title: Time Capsule to Future Me
goal: Your kid packs a record of right now for the person they'll be in a few years. They survey real prices, cut a paper strip to their exact height, trace their hand and foot, ask everyone at home the same questions, write predictions and a letter to future them, then seal it with an opening date and a small ceremony.
need: A box, tin or large envelope that closes well
A receipt, a flyer or a trip to a store for real prices
A long strip of paper, scissors, a tape measure and a pencil
Paper for letters and interviews, and a phone to record if you like

levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

howTo.intro: Ordinary things are what future them will find most surprising: the price of bread, the size of a hand, what a sibling said at dinner. Push for exact numbers and real words instead of 'stuff I like', and take part yourself, because your answers go in the box too.

plan.what: Measure, then interview the family (Steps 2 and 3).
Write, predict and seal it (Steps 4 and 5).

troubleshoot.q: They want to open it next week
troubleshoot.a: Meet in the middle. One year, on their next birthday, is long enough for a 6-year-old to notice real changes. Older kids can choose five years.
Ask for an example: 'What's your favourite food right now, and when did you last eat it?' A story is easier to give than a list.

troubleshoot.q: We'll forget where we put it
troubleshoot.a: Write the place and the opening date on the calendar, and in a note on your phone, the day you seal it.

lesson.text: A time capsule is a message to a reader who doesn't exist yet: the older version of your kid. What future them will want most is exact, everyday detail, numbers they can check and words in people's own voices, and a few predictions to find out if they were right.
lesson.before: 'I'll put in my favourite toy and a drawing.'

model.line: Milk $2.50 for 1 litre, a pizza slice $3, bus ticket $2.75.
A paper strip 128 cm long, a traced hand, a traced foot, shoe size 1.
Five people, same four questions, answers written down word for word.
'I'll be about 140 cm, because kids grow around 6 cm a year.'

lesson.modelNote: 'A toy and a drawing' tells future them what they liked. Prices, a strip of paper and five sets of answers give them things to measure against, so opening day becomes a comparison instead of just a memory.

steps.title: Survey the prices
steps.why: A real price list now makes real math on opening day.
steps.kid: Your kid picks 8 to 10 everyday things, like milk, bread, a banana, a stamp, a bus ticket and their favourite treat, and writes down the exact price and size of each, using the Price survey card in the Time Capsule Toolkit at the end of the guide.
steps.you: Take them to the store or hand them this week's receipt. Help them read the size on the label, so the same item can be compared later.
ask: Which price do you think will go up the most?
steps.tip: Add a flyer, or a photocopy of the receipt. Shop receipts fade over the years, but a copy or a flyer stays readable.

levels.explore: Pick five things at the store, and help a parent write down each price.
levels.develop: Survey 8 to 10 items with exact prices and sizes, and guess each future price.
levels.extend: Ask a grandparent what three of the items cost when they were your age, and work out how many times higher the price is now.

steps.title: Measure me now
steps.why: Kids never see themselves grow. A paper strip to unroll later makes it something to hold.
steps.kid: Your kid stands against a wall while you mark their height, then cuts a paper strip exactly that long and writes the date on it. They trace their hand and their foot, and record shoe size and arm span, using the Measure me card.
steps.you: Make the height mark with a book flat on their head. Measure twice, and let them read the tape measure.
ask: How much taller do you think you'll be when it opens?
Is your arm span longer or shorter than your height?
steps.tip: Roll the strip loosely instead of folding it. Folds crack paper over the years.

levels.explore: Trace your hand and your foot, and help cut your height strip.
levels.develop: Measure your height, arm span and shoe size, and cut the strip exactly.
levels.extend: Use about 6 cm a year to predict your height when it opens, and mark that prediction on your strip in a second colour.

steps.title: Ask everyone the same questions
steps.why: Same questions for everyone make a family snapshot, and a fair comparison later.
steps.kid: Your kid picks four questions from the Family snapshot card and asks every person at home, plus anyone else they'd like, writing the answers word for word or recording them. One question is always about the future: 'What do you think I'll be like when this opens?'
steps.you: Answer properly when it's your turn. Help with spelling or recording, and keep each interview short, five minutes at most.
ask: Which question do you want to ask them again on opening day?
steps.tip: If you record on a phone, write the answers down too. Paper will open in ten years; a file might not.

levels.explore: Ask two people one question each, and draw their answers.
levels.develop: Ask four questions to everyone at home, and write the answers word for word.
levels.extend: Answer the four questions yourself, then predict how each person's answer will change by the time you open it.

steps.title: Predict and write to future me
steps.why: A prediction with a reason is a real test of how well they understand the world now.
steps.kid: Your kid writes five predictions for opening day, each with a reason and how sure they are, using the Predictions card. Then they write a letter using the Letter to future me card: who they are now, what's hard, what they hope, and one question for future them.
steps.you: Ask 'Why do you think that?' after each prediction. Write your own short letter to them, to open on the same day.
ask: Which prediction are you most sure about?
What question do you want future you to answer?
steps.tip: Specific predictions are more fun to check. 'Milk will cost $3.10' beats 'things will cost more'.

levels.explore: Say three things you think will be different, and draw a picture of future you.
levels.develop: Write five predictions with reasons, and a one-page letter.
levels.extend: Rate each prediction from 1 to 10 for how sure you are, and write what would have to happen to prove you wrong.

steps.title: Pack it and seal it
steps.why: A date and a ceremony turn a box of papers into something they'll wait for.
steps.kid: Your kid chooses the opening date and packs everything, using the Pack and open card. They write the date and 'Do not open until' on the outside, then seal it with a small ceremony they design: everyone signs the lid, says one wish, or watches it go into its hiding place.
steps.you: Help find a cool, dry spot inside the home, away from heaters. Put the opening date in your calendar while they watch.
ask: Why did you choose that date?
What do you think you'll check first when you open it?
steps.tip: Leave out batteries, food and anything with rubber. They break down and can ruin the paper.

levels.explore: Help pack the box, and sign the lid with the whole family.
levels.develop: Pick the date, pack it carefully, and run the sealing ceremony.
levels.extend: Write the opening-day instructions: what to compare first, and how to work out each price change as a percent.

conclusion.headline: They sent a message to the person they'll grow into.
conclusion.text: Keep the opening date somewhere you'll both see it. In the months after, notice when they mention a price, a measurement or a prediction from the box, because that's them already checking it against the world.
conclusion.celebrate: When the lid is signed and sealed, say: 'Future you is going to open this and meet exactly who you are today.'
extensions: Make a second, tiny capsule to open in just one month, and test your short-term predictions
Run the same price survey in another town or country you visit, and compare the two lists
Make a capsule for a younger sibling or cousin, with their measurements and your predictions about them
Plan the opening day now: who comes, what you'll eat, and which question you'll ask everyone again

signs: They notice and mention what things cost
They back up predictions with a reason
They talk about who they're becoming, not only who they are
makeItReal: On your next grocery run, hand your kid the receipt at the checkout and ask which three prices they'd want to remember in five years.

classroom.intro: A class time capsule is a classic for good reason. Each student fills their own envelope, the class adds a few shared pages, and everything goes into one box to open at the end of the year or later.

tips.d: Bring in grocery flyers and a few store web pages rather than family receipts. Small groups fill in the Price survey card for eight items, writing the exact price and size of each.
Partners trace hands and feet, measure arm span and cut a dated height strip using the Measure me card. Kids who'd rather not be measured at school can do it at home.
In class, students ask four Family snapshot questions to classmates instead of family. Asking the same questions at home is optional homework, never required.
The Letter to future me goes into a sealed envelope with the student's name on it. Tell students nobody will read it, and keep that promise.
Explore kids say three things that will change and draw future them, Develop kids write five predictions with reasons, and Extend kids rate how sure they are.
Everyone signs the lid and says one wish. Store the box somewhere cool and dry at school with a clear opening date, or send each envelope home to keep.

classroom.timing: Plan four sessions of about 40 minutes: prices, measuring, interviews, then predictions, letters and sealing. Family interviews are optional homework, and each envelope can go home to keep if the class box won't stay at school.
